extracted.intended_audience: readers of detective/mystery fiction; anyone interested in principles of investigating a disappearance (as portrayed in fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, evidence-focused steps and reasoning for investigating a mysterious disappearance (as represented in the narrative): examine physical means of exit, corroborate witness testimony, evaluate motives, and distinguish staged or supernatural explanations from material evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine all possible physical exits
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically check every plausible way the missing person could have left (doors, windows, chimney, bathroom, secret passages, panels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanley taps walls, inspects the chimney and bathroom, and rules out windows (third-story, only opened a few inches). Quote examples: 'No exit but the door,--so far as appears on the surface.' 'A monkey couldn't negotiate that,' (re: chimney). The investigator concludes that if no physical exit exists, other inferences must be drawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for secret entrances and hollow panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate thoroughly for hidden passages, panels, or other structural routes that might explain an apparently impossible departure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanley 'sounded and tested every bit of wall' and tapped partitions and paper to detect secret doors; Harbison suggests seeking hollow panels as a non-supernatural source of 'voices' and strange sounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect locks and bolts for tampering or fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how doors and bolts were left — consider whether locks/bolts were genuinely secured or intentionally staged to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsie hypothesizes that the 'broken lock and burst bolt are fabrications to mislead investigators.' The detectives solicit testimony from servants about the difficulty entering the room to corroborate the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for and preserve physical traces/clues in the room
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for marks, residues, disturbed or cleaned areas, missing objects, and clothing arrangements that may indicate struggle, theft, or staging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsie notes 'white daubs' on the carpet (like chalk), the room having been cleaned, bed made, chiffonier tidied, and missing diamonds. These specifics are used to generate hypotheses about what happened and whether the scene was altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a precise timeline and canvass neighbors
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the time window during which the disappearance could have occurred and ask nearby neighbors or occupants if they observed anything during that window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanley frames the possible exit as between 'two A. M. and, say, seven' and suggests asking the Thornes and other neighbors if they saw anything. Timing is used to narrow witness canvass and possible sighting opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate and cross-check witness testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview and cross-validate accounts from servants, family members, and other witnesses; note inconsistencies and possible prevarications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The butler and chauffeur are summoned to corroborate events; Oscar reports hearing Miss Webb say something that Henrietta denies. Hanley stresses confirmation by 'credible witnesses.' Discrepancies (e.g., Henrietta's denials vs. others' statements) become salient evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and investigate plausible motives and suspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerate people who might benefit or have motive (family members, professional rivals) and test hypotheses linking motive to opportunity and method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harbison proposes Wallace Courtney (a fellow playwright) had motive (fear of plagiarism). Elsie suspects Henrietta and reasons about family incentives tied to inheritance. Motive is weighed alongside physical possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismiss improbable or absurd details — use them to generate hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat seemingly ridiculous or contradictory facts as diagnostic clues that can narrow possibilities or reveal staging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsie points out the absurdity that Kimball allegedly left wearing evening clothes and carrying pajamas but no morning suit; she argues such absurdities should 'point to some inevitable conclusion' rather than be ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize material evidence over supernatural explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertain supernatural or folkloric explanations only insofar as they are supported by credible, corroborated testimony; maintain a presumption toward physical explanations unless evidence compels otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs. Webb invokes spiritist explanations ('the passing of matter through matter'), but Hanley and others treat such claims skeptically: 'This is interesting only if confirmed by credible witnesses.' Harbison prefers to seek a secret passage rather than accept levitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage affected parties but coordinate with official investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow interested parties (fiancée, family) to assist or provide leads, but work collaboratively with official detectives and respect investigative roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsie insists on helping and Hanley accepts collaboration: 'Together, miss, by all means. I'll be only too glad of any help you can give me.' The narrative emphasizes usefulness of local knowledge alongside professional methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider theft or burglary as alternate explanations when valuables are missing
rubrics_metrics.description: If valuables are unaccounted for, investigate whether theft provides motive and whether the disappearance could be a cover for burglary or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanley raises the possibility of burglary because 'the diamonds are not to be found' and notes their high value; Elsie counters that Kim may have them. The missing pendant introduces alternative theories (robbery, abduction for theft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use press/publicity dynamics as investigative context
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that public attention affects behavior and evidence preservation; consider how publicity may influence suspects' actions or witnesses' statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hanley warns the family that 'the papers will be full of it for nine days, at least,' implying that publicity is a practical factor in the investigation and may complicate concealment or staging.
